newsitem.title: INDIA: Market forces should determine interest - RBI chief.
newsitem.headline: Market forces should determine interest - RBI chief.

text.p: Interest rates should be determined by the forces of demand and supply, the governor of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said on Monday.

"It has been argued that when market forces are allowed to determine the rate of interest, the rate will tend to remain high and such high rates can hinder the process of growth," RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan said in Bangalore.

High interest rates, among other factors, were blamed for poor credit offtake by the industry last year. The RBI took several steps to increase lendable resources and prompt lending rate cuts in its monetary policy announced late last year.

"But these critics fail to understand that if rates of interest are kept at artifically low levels, it can only result in diverting funds from the organised sector to the unorganised sectors, losing total control over the end-use of funds."

While aggregate savings may not be significantly influenced by changes in interest rate, there is enough evidence to show -- even in the Indian context -- that savings in the form of financial assets are considerably influenced by interest rates, Rangarajan told a meeting.
A copy of the governor's speech was sent to Reuters by RBI.
If financial institutions are to perform their major role of mobilising resources, the interest rate should be allowed to be determined by the forces of demand and supply, he said.
But he admitted that the interest rate was a strategic variable and its level can be and is influenced by the actions of the monetary authority.
"In that sense, interest rate nowhere in the world is purely determined by market forces," Rangarajan said.
"The monetary authority cannot keep interest rates for long at levels athat are inconsistent with the basic supply and demand balance," he said.
Over a time, the only way to keep the nominal interest low is to maintain the inflation rate at a reasonably low level.
"It is sometimes argued that high rates of interest that the government has to pay on its borrowings worsens the fiscal deficit," the governor said.

"But it is overlooked that high interest rates themselves are not the cause but the effect of unduly large fiscal deficits -- the answer to reducing the interest payments lies basically in the government containing the fiscal deficit," he added.
